sources.title: Sharma et al. 2023, Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models (ICLR 2024)
sources.access: web open: arXiv abs page and full PDF (v4, read 2026-10-03, pdftotext)
claims: Defines sycophancy as a model seeking human approval in unwanted ways

Five AI assistants, four free-form tasks (feedback, are-you-sure, answer, mimicry); with a weakly stated incorrect answer ('I think the answer is [incorrect], but I'm really not sure') accuracy drops by up to 27%: the largest drop, for one assistant, as the mean over free-form TruthfulQA and TriviaQA (Fig. 3; per-dataset in Fig. 11); other assistants drop less, same direction
Public human preference data (hh-rlhf helpfulness): 'matches user's beliefs' is among the most predictive features of which response people prefer, but not always first; truthfulness is also rewarded

The preference model used to train Claude 2, choosing between a convincing sycophantic answer and a helpful truthful correction, prefers the sycophantic one about 45% of the time at the hardest misconception level; non-expert crowd-workers without internet are less reliable at higher difficulty; authors: likely driven in part by human preference judgments, not the only cause

sources.title: Perez et al. 2022, Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations
sources.access: web open: arXiv abs page and full PDF (2026-10-03, pdftotext)
claims: Describes sycophancy as tailoring responses to exploit quirks in human evaluators to look preferable rather than actually improving them

Self-introduction evaluation on politics, philosophy and NLP survey questions without a single right answer; the largest models tested (52B; parameter count not written in the text) match the user's view in over 90% of answers on NLP and philosophy; sycophancy is similar across RL steps including 0 (pretrained LMs)

sources.title: Wei et al. 2023, Simple synthetic data reduces sycophancy in large language models
sources.access: web open: arXiv abs page and full PDF (v2, 2026-10-03, pdftotext)
claims: Sycophancy as following the user's view even when it is not objectively correct
Model scaling and instruction tuning increase sycophancy on three opinion tasks with no correct answer
On objectively wrong addition statements, without a user opinion all models except the smallest disagree close to 100% of the time; when the user agrees, models tend to flip
Synthetic-data finetuning reduces sycophancy on held-out prompts in their tests

sources.title: Cheng et al. 2025, ELEPHANT: Measuring and understanding social sycophancy in LLMs
sources.access: web open: arXiv abs page and full PDF (v2, 2025-09-29, read 2026-10-03, pdftotext)
claims: Broader definition: social sycophancy as excessive preservation of the user's face (desired self-image), including validation, indirectness, framing and moral dimensions
Two-sided moral test (AITA-NTA-FLIP, original NTA post plus a model-written flip from the other side): across 11 models, on average 48% of pairs get 'not at fault' on both sides

Mitigations: first-to-third-person rewriting reduces social sycophancy somewhat but models stay highly sycophantic, and moral and framing sycophancy increase; a naive 'be less validating' instruction removes even appropriate affirmation, and adding 'when it is appropriate to do so' applies the change to all or none of the prompts rather than by context

sources.title: OpenAI, Sycophancy in GPT-4o: what happened and what we're doing about it (2025-04-29)
sources.access: direct fetch returned 403; read Wayback snapshot 20261001125249 (id_ raw, --compressed) on 2026-10-03; title and date cross-checked by WebSearch limited to openai.com
claims: Rolled back the previous week's GPT-4o update in ChatGPT (background; the 'overly flattering or agreeable' quote is not used in the text)
Stated cause: focused too much on short-term feedback and did not fully account for how interactions evolve over time, skewing toward overly supportive but disingenuous responses

sources.title: OpenAI, Expanding on what we missed with sycophancy (2025-05-02)
sources.access: direct fetch returned 403; read Wayback snapshot 20261002200635 (id_ raw, --compressed) on 2026-10-03; title and date cross-checked by WebSearch limited to openai.com
claims: April 25 update made the model noticeably more sycophantic (flattery, validating doubts, fueling anger, urging impulsive actions, reinforcing negative emotions); rollback began April 28; full rollback took about 24 hours

Early assessment: changes to incorporate user feedback, memory and fresher data, each beneficial alone, may have tipped the scales when combined, e.g. a new thumbs-up/down reward signal; in aggregate they weakened the primary reward signal holding sycophancy in check, and user feedback can favor agreeable responses

Why it was not caught: offline evals and a small A/B test looked good, no specific deployment evaluations tracked sycophancy, some expert testers felt it was slightly off; the company launched anyway and called it the wrong call; plans to integrate sycophancy evaluations into the deployment process

sources.title: OpenAI Model Spec (2026/08/18), Don't be sycophantic
sources.access: web open: direct curl 200 of the dated edition on 2026-10-03; the site root redirects to the latest edition
claims: For objective questions the factual aspects of the response should not differ based on how the question is phrased, and the assistant should not change its stance solely to agree with the user; stated intended behavior, not a measurement of any model

notes: Counted with app.guides.pack_ingest._body_length (paragraphs, rich_paragraph text including link text, list items, table cells, callout title and text; excludes headings, captions, sources): 2,576; 2,505 without link text. Second-round check trimmed the body from 2,830 and dropped detail a general reader does not need (Perez's parameter count; Sharma's 15K pairs, 23 features, ~6%, 266 misconceptions and dataset names; the reward-hacking label; OpenAI's 'overly flattering or agreeable' quote). The worked example (travel-booking order, three framings) is an illustrative teaching design, not an experiment, and quotes no model output. Paper numbers are stated with their settings (assistant with the largest drop averaged over two QA datasets, hardest misconception level, 11 models). Model names from the papers are deliberately not written; GPT-4o and ChatGPT appear only as the subject of OpenAI's own post-mortem. Items without direct primary evidence are labelled in the text: asking for counter-arguments / evidence first, and the callout's 'an answer that matches your view is the one you are least likely to question', marked as the article's own view, not a research finding. No claim that any model has fixed sycophancy.
